turns.userMessage: Conversation info (untrusted metadata): ```json { "message_id": "8324", "sender_id": "8518484672", "conversation_label": "BOUNTIFUL id:-5151316478", "sender": "Jonathan", "timestamp": "Tue 2026-03-03 13:36 PST", "group_subject": "BOUNTIFUL", "is_group_chat": true } ``` Sender (untrusted metadata): ```json { "label": "Jonathan (8518484672)", "id": "8518484672", "name": "Jonathan" } ``` We need way more green for everything that can be green. To make every park-ish thing read “lush green” in Mapbox, the trick is: parks are not just one layer. In Mapbox Streets, “green areas” are spread across landuse + landuse_overlay + landcover (and sometimes “wood/forest/grass” lives in a different layer than “park”). Here’s the playbook that reliably gets Presidio + GGP + neighborhood parks + golf courses + cemeteries + sports fields all green. --- 1) Find where your “green” is actually coming from In Mapbox Studio → Styles → your style → Layers: Use the layer search box for: landuse, landuse_overlay, landcover, park, national, wood, grass, pitch, cemetery, golf, recreation Then use Inspect (cursor icon) and click: A spot inside GGP A spot inside Presidio A random small neighborhood park Look at the feature properties. You’re usually matching on one of these: class subclass sometimes type (less common) sometimes name is present but you shouldn’t rely on it This tells you which layer + which class values you must catch. --- 2) Don’t “tweak existing park layers” — add one super-layer that overrides all park-ish polygons Create a new fill layer (this is the “crank it up” layer) and place it: ✅ Above landuse/landcover fills ✅ Below road casings / road fills / labels (so streets stay crisp) Example (Style JSON) — one “Parks Unified” fill layer { "id": "parks-unified-fill", "type": "fill", "source": "composite", "source-layer": "landuse", "filter": [ "any", ["match", ["get", "class"], ["park","national_park","pitch","grass","cemetery","golf_course","playground","recreation_ground","nature_reserve","protected_area","allotments"], true, false ] ], "paint": { "fill-color": "#0B5A2A", "fill-opacity": 0.55 } } Then duplicate that same idea for landuse_overlay (because a lot of “park” polygons show up there in some styles): { "id": "parks-unified-fill-overlay", "type": "fill", "source": "composite", "source-layer": "landuse_overlay", "filter": [ "any", ["match", ["get", "class"], ["park","national_park","pitch","grass","cemetery","golf_course","playground","recreation_ground","nature_reserve","protected_area","allotments"], true, false ] ], "paint": { "fill-color": "#0B5A2A", "fill-opacity": 0.55 } } And if you still see “green-ish natural areas” staying beige, that’s usually landcover (woods/forest/scrub): { "id": "parks-unified-landcover", "type": "fill", "source": "composite", "source-layer": "landcover", "filter": [ "match", ["get", "class"], ["wood","forest","grass","scrub","wetland"], true, false ], "paint": { "fill-color": "#0B5A2A", "fill-opacity": 0.45 } } That 3-layer combo is usually the “aha”: GGP/Presidio often hit landcover (wood/forest) in addition to landuse (park/national_park). --- 3) Add a subtle outline so shapes feel intentional (and “more green”) Add a line layer using the same filters, placed above your unified fills: { "id": "parks-unified-outline", "type": "line", "source": "composite", "source-layer": "landuse", "filter": [ "match", ["get", "class"], ["park","national_park","pitch","cemetery","golf_course","playground","recreation_ground","nature_reserve","protected_area"], true, false ], "paint": { "line-color": "#06411E", "line-width": 1.2, "line-opacity": 0.6 } } (You can do the same for landuse_overlay if needed.) --- 4) If it’s still “not green enough”: crank saturation without making roads muddy Instead of only raising opacity, keep opacity moderate but choose a deeper green and optionally use slight contrast: Try fill-color: #0A6B2F or #075024 Push fill-opacity toward 0.60–0.70 for landuse/overlay Keep landcover slightly lower (like 0.35–0.50) so it doesn’t overpower everything Also: make sure your unified layers are above the base landuse/landcover layers—otherwise you’re tweaking the wrong thing. --- 5) Common “missing green” classes to includeThese are the usual culprits when someone says “we’re missing something”: national_park protected_area nature_reserve recreation_ground playground pitch (sports fields) golf_course cemetery grass wood / forest (landcover) If Presidio/GGP won’t turn green, it’s almost always because you only styled park but the feature is actually national_park or it’s coming from landcover wood/forest. --- 6) Quick debugging checklist (fast) 1. Click Presidio inside polygon → which source-layer? (landuse vs landcover vs landuse_overlay) 2. What is class exactly? 3. Is your new layer above the layer currently painting that polygon? 4. Are you accidentally only editing one of (landuse, landuse_overlay, landcover)? --- If you paste (or screenshot) the Inspect panel output for a click inside Presidio + a click inside a small park (showing source-layer + class/subclass), I can tell you exactly which classes/layers you’re missing and the minimal filter list to catch 100% of parks in your current style.
